identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Chottanikkara Devi Temple, in Ernakulam district, worships the goddess as Rajarajeswari in three forms through the day — as Saraswathi in the morning, Lakshmi at noon and Kali (or Durga, in some sources) in the evening. Wikipedia describes the central image as a self-manifested (svayambhu) laterite formation. The temple is closely associated with the Guruthi and related rituals performed at its adjoining Kizhukkavu shrine, which devotees believe can help with mental distress; this is a devotional belief rather than a clinical claim, and is reported here as such.

governance.establishedEra: Kerala Tourism states the temple dates to the early 10th century CE; this is a tourism-page claim rather than an archaeologically documented date

narrative.summaryIntro: Chottanikkara Devi Temple, about 18 km from Kochi in Ernakulam district, is one of Kerala's most visited goddess temples. The presiding deity, worshipped as Rajarajeswari, is venerated in three forms across the day: as Saraswathi in the morning, Lakshmi at noon, and Kali or Durga (sources differ on the evening form) in the evening. Wikipedia describes the deity as a self-manifested laterite formation known as the Rudraksha Sila, and records that an image of Mahavishnu shares the same pedestal, giving rise to the combined names Lakshmi Narayana and Amme Narayana. The temple, managed by the Cochin Devaswom Board, is closely associated with the Guruthi ritual performed at its adjoining Kizhukkavu (Keezhkkavu) shrine to Bhadrakali, which devotees regard as helpful for mental and spiritual distress. Its principal annual festival, Makam Thozhal, is held in the Malayalam month of Kumbham.
narrative.sthalaPuranam: Wikipedia records a temple legend involving a tribesman, Kannappan, who lived in the surrounding forest and performed ritual buffalo sacrifices. After his daughter Pavizham died following an incident involving a calf, the sacrificial altar is said to have revealed a divine presence in its place, which a priest explained as the divine couple Vishnu and Lakshmi manifest in the form of the calf. The temple's own site further states that the goddess appeared to the sage Vilwamangalam Swamiyar, an event commemorated annually at the Makam Thozhal festival.
narrative.documentedHistory: The temple is administered by the Cochin Devaswom Board, which the Board's own site describes as overseeing several hundred temples across Ernakulam, Thrissur and Palakkad districts, with Chottanikkara among its most significant shrines. The Cochin Devaswom Board's site also describes the Bhadrakali deity at the adjoining Kizhukkavu shrine as believed to help free devotees from distress after bhajanam (devotional singing) is performed; this is reported here as a devotional belief documented by the managing board, not as a medical claim.

visitingInfo.officialContactNote: The temple's own site states general opening and closing times but notes variation on Fridays and during the Mandalam season; confirm same-day darshan and Guruthi/vazhipadu timings with the temple before travelling.

openingHours.notes: The temple's own site states the temple opens at 4:00 am generally (3:30 am during the Mandalam season and on Fridays) and closes after the evening Seeveli, around 8:30 pm. Treat the closing time as approximate.
